title: Nada (Ascent of Mount Carmel)
hookLine: his drawing of the mountain: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing

cards: A friar sits down and draws a mountain for a convent of nuns. Paths wind up it, with words written along them. It's John, after his escape.
He's been sent south, and in the town of Beas he visits the Carmelite nuns as their confessor and teacher. So he does something teachers still do: he draws a diagram.
He makes copies and hands them out, so each nun can keep one in her breviary. And written again and again up the middle path is today's word.

teach.b: First, the two wide roads. On the left and right of John's mountain are broad paths. One is labeled with the goods of earth: possessions, pleasure, knowledge, comfort.
The other with the goods of heaven: glory, joy, consolation, even spiritual rewards. Both look sensible. Both wind around and stop short of the top.

teach.h: NADA, NADA, NADA UP THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: Straight up the middle runs a thin path, and on it John writes one Spanish word, over and over: nada, nada, nada, nada. Nothing. And near the top: and even on the mountain, nothing.

Third, the verses. Beside the drawing, and later in his book the Ascent of Mount Carmel, John writes lines that turn on this word. In his Spanish: "Para venir a gustarlo todo, no quieras tener gusto en nada."

teach.h: TO ENJOY ALL, CLING TO NOTHING.
teach.b: To come to enjoy everything, desire to have enjoyment in nothing.
To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to be everything, desire to be nothing. Fourth, what it means.
It sounds bleak. It isn't meant to be. John isn't saying the world is bad, or that people don't matter.
His point is about grasping. Cling to anything, even good things, even spiritual things, and your hands are full.

teach.h: NO QUIERAS TENER GUSTO EN NADA.
teach.b: Nada is emptying the hands. And the promise at the top of the drawing isn't nothing. It's everything, which is God.
Nothing, then everything: the order is the lesson.

how: Carmelites and many Catholics study John's sketch of Mount Carmel and the nada verses from the Ascent, often as a guide to detachment in Lent or on retreat.

o: a belief that the world and its pleasures are evil
a vow to give away every last thing you own to the poor
Spanish for nothing: letting go of grasping, even good things

games.q: what's on the mountain — tap the pairs.
p: a wide road that stops short

s: John drew his mountain for the nuns he taught
for the Carmelite nuns at Beas, with copies to keep.
nada means the world is bad
John's point is about grasping. clinging to anything, even good things, fills the hands.
on John's drawing, the road of spiritual rewards reaches the top
even the goods of heaven, sought for themselves, stop short. only the narrow path of nada goes up.

games.q: you're climbing John's mountain. one road promises comfort, another promises spiritual joys, and a thin path up the middle says nothing, nothing, nothing. which do you take?
games.why: on John's drawing only the narrow path of nada reaches the top, where he promises everything, which is God.

practice: Open your hands on your knees, palms up, and think of one thing you've been wanting hard: a purchase, a result, someone's approval, even a certain feeling in prayer.
Picture it resting in your open hands, and stop gripping; you don't have to throw it away. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, notice how open hands feel.

wordCard.voice: Nada. Spanish for nothing, written up the narrow path on John's drawing of Mount Carmel: cling to nothing, and at the top, God, who is everything. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish: nothing. from Latin (res) nata, a thing born, used in 'not a thing'.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing, then everything. Empty hands have room for what John promises at the top. See you tomorrow.
